evidence.text: Look for. • Category selection mechanics: Target existing, massive categories so you do not have to educate the consumer on what the product is. Look for a "sea of sameness" where all incumbents look identical (e.g., all dish soaps are green and toxic; all vitamins are round and pseudo-scientific). • Cultural shift mapping: Identify a macro trend happening elsewhere (e.g., "boutique fitness as a spiritual pursuit") and apply it to the stagnant category (e.g., daily vitamins) to create "creative tension." • Cross-industry theft mechanics: Steal aesthetics from completely unrelated industries. The further apart the dots, the more powerful the idea (e.g., stealing high-end houseware vase shapes and applying them to dish soap packaging). • The "One Iteration" Rule: Change exactly ONE major variable from the core product expectation. If you change two or three things simultaneously, the product becomes "too novel," breaking consumer adoption. • Naming constraints: The holy grail of brand naming is one word, four letters. Identify a core "jumping-off word" based on the product's ultimate goal (e.g., "technique" for cleaning -> Method; "friendly" for vitamins -> Olly), and base the naming search purely on that feeling.

evidence_quotes: The "One Iteration" Rule: Change exactly ONE major variable from the core product expectation.
